hook: Your child isn't bad at maths. They're two topics behind.

points.heading: It's almost always the same two
points.body: Fractions in Year 7. Negative numbers in Year 8. Across the Cambridge and IGCSE students our mentors work with, the ones who say they aren't a maths person have nearly always lost one or both.

points.heading: Everything after that looks like weakness
points.body: Once fractions are shaky, ratio breaks. Then algebra. Then trigonometry. By Year 10 it reads as ability. It is arithmetic nobody was given time to finish.

points.heading: Marks hide the cause
points.body: A report says 42 percent. It does not say which four topics produced it. That is why work harder rarely moves the number - the effort goes to the wrong place.

points.heading: Find the line, not the grade
points.body: Our mentors work backwards through the curriculum until the answers stop being wrong. That point is the real starting line, and it is usually three or four topics earlier than parents expect.

points.heading: Two topics is a term, not a year
points.body: Closing a genuine gap takes weeks, not a rebuild. The reason it feels impossible is that nobody has named which two.

caption:
Two topics. That is usually the whole story.

Fractions in Year 7. Negative numbers in Year 8. Across the Cambridge and IGCSE students our mentors work with, the ones who say they are not a maths person have nearly always lost one or both.

Everything after that looks like weakness. It is arithmetic nobody finished.

Ask your child which question made them feel that way. Start there.

Confidence is not a personality.

No child is born without it in maths. It is lost in a specific term, on a specific topic, usually without anyone noticing.

Which means it can be found again. That is the whole method.

hook: Three questions to ask on a school tour that the brochure won't answer.

points.heading: What happens when a student falls behind
points.body: Not the policy. The actual sequence of events. Who notices, in which week, and what changes on the timetable. Most schools cannot answer this in specifics.

points.heading: How many dropped A Level Maths last year
points.body: The number after Year 12 tells you more about teaching quality than any league table. Schools that teach it well do not lose students at that point.

points.heading: Who teaches the bottom set
points.body: Strong departments put experienced teachers with the students who are struggling. Weak ones give them to whoever is free.

cta: Save this before your next school tour.
caption:
The brochure will not answer these.

1. What actually happens when a student falls behind in maths - the sequence, not the policy.
2. How many students dropped A Level Mathematics after Year 12 last year.
3. Who teaches the bottom set.

Our mentors have run these tours from the other side of the table. These three tell you more than the whole visit.

hook: Fractions in Year 7. Negative numbers in Year 8.
caption:
The two topics that decide everything after them.

Fractions in Year 7. Negative numbers in Year 8. Lose either and ratio, algebra and trigonometry all inherit the gap.

It is not ability. It is sequence.

hook: What a maths report actually tells you, and what it hides.

points.heading: A percentage is an average of averages
points.body: 62 percent could be strong algebra and collapsed geometry, or steady mediocrity across everything. The two need completely different responses, and the number cannot tell them apart.

points.heading: 'Could apply himself more' usually means something specific
points.body: Ask which topic the teacher was thinking of when they wrote it. Nine times out of ten there is one concrete moment behind that sentence.

points.heading: Effort grades measure compliance, not learning
points.body: A child who is quietly lost often scores well on effort. They are working hard on the wrong thing, which is the most expensive kind of hard work.

points.heading: Ask for the question-level breakdown
points.body: Most schools have it and rarely send it. It shows exactly which topics cost the marks, which is the only thing you can actually act on.

cta: Save this before the next report evening.
caption:
A maths report is an average of averages.

62 percent could be strong algebra and collapsed geometry, or steady mediocrity everywhere. Those need opposite responses, and the number cannot tell them apart.

Ask for the question-level breakdown. Most schools have it and rarely send it.

That one request changes the conversation.

hook: Working hard on the wrong topic is still working hard.
sub: It just doesn't move the grade.
caption:
Working hard on the wrong topic is still working hard.

It is the most expensive kind of effort, because the child pays for it in confidence and sees nothing back.

Before more hours, find the gap. Then the hours count.

hook: IGCSE or IB Maths - which actually opens more doors?

points.heading: Neither, on its own
points.body: Universities read the grade and the depth, not the acronym. A strong IGCSE record beats a scraped IB one at every admissions desk we have dealt with.

points.heading: The real question is teaching depth
points.body: Ask how many periods a week the school gives to maths, and who teaches the top set. That predicts outcomes far better than the curriculum badge.

points.heading: IB rewards breadth, IGCSE rewards precision
points.body: A child who likes closing a problem cleanly often thrives in IGCSE. One who enjoys connecting ideas across subjects tends to prefer IB.

points.heading: Switching later is harder than parents expect
points.body: The two build sequence differently. A mid-stream move usually costs a term of catching up, so choose for the child you have, not the one you hope for.

Your child is not behind.

A topic was left unfinished, and everything built on top of it inherited the gap.

That is a sequence problem, not an ability problem. Sequence problems have solutions.

hook: The five-minute check that tells you where the gap is.

points.heading: Ask them to explain, not to solve
points.body: Give a question they got right and ask why the method works. Fluency without understanding shows up in seconds, and it is the single best early warning.

points.heading: Go back two years, not two weeks
points.body: Set a question from Year 7 fractions. If it is slow or uncertain, you have found the floor, and no amount of Year 10 revision will fix it.

points.heading: Watch where they stop, not what they answer
points.body: The pause tells you more than the mark. Children hesitate exactly at the topic they never closed.

points.heading: Do it without a grade attached
points.body: The moment it feels like a test, you measure anxiety instead of knowledge. Keep it casual and the information is far better.

cta: Try this tonight. It takes five minutes.
caption:
Five minutes, and no marking.

Give your child a question they got right, and ask them why the method works. Fluency without understanding shows up almost immediately.

Then set one from two years earlier. Watch where they pause, not what they answer.

The hesitation is the diagnosis.

The pause is the diagnosis.

Children hesitate at exactly the topic they never closed. The mark tells you there is a problem. The hesitation tells you where.

Watch for it. It is more useful than any report.

hook: Four questions to ask a tutor before you pay anything.

points.heading: What will you do in the first session?
points.body: If the answer is 'start the syllabus', walk away. The first session should be diagnosis. Nobody can teach a gap they have not located.

points.heading: How will I know it is working?
points.body: A good tutor names a measure before they start. 'Confidence' is not a measure. 'She will close negative numbers in three weeks' is.

points.heading: What happens when she gets stuck?
points.body: Listen for whether they explain again louder, or go backwards to find the missing step. Only one of those is teaching.

points.heading: Who else have you taught at this level?
points.body: IGCSE and A Level Mathematics are specific. General maths tutoring is not the same job, and the difference shows by week three.

cta: Ask these before the first invoice.
caption:
Four questions before you pay a tutor anything.

1. What will you do in the first session? If the answer is 'start the syllabus', walk away.
2. How will I know it is working?
3. What happens when she gets stuck?
4. Who else have you taught at this level?

The first answer tells you most of what you need.

hook: The first session should be diagnosis.
caption:
The first session should be diagnosis, not chapter one.

Nobody can teach a gap they have not located. Starting the syllabus on day one assumes the problem is coverage. It almost never is.

Ask any tutor what they will do first. The answer tells you everything.

hook: The Year 9 decision most parents make by accident.

points.heading: Set placement in Year 9 shapes Year 12
points.body: The tier a child is entered for narrows what they can take at A Level. That decision is often made on one year of marks, quietly, by a timetable.

points.heading: Foundation tier caps the grade
points.body: Many parents do not realise the ceiling exists until results day. Ask which tier your child is on track for, and ask now, not in Year 11.

points.heading: Movement between sets is possible but rare
points.body: Schools will move a child up if the evidence is loud. That means closing gaps early enough for the evidence to exist.

points.heading: The window is roughly eighteen months
points.body: From the start of Year 9 to the tier decision. Long enough to change the outcome, short enough that drifting through it costs you.

caption:

hook: The ceiling is set earlier than results day.
